title: The RBI Meets This Week. Every Economist Expects It to Do Nothing. That May Be the Point.
excerpt: The central bank is expected to hold rates at 5.25 percent on Friday. But with oil above $90, the rupee near 95, and inflation rising, the real signal will be in what it says next.
body:
The Reserve Bank of India's Monetary Policy Committee begins a three-day meeting on Tuesday, and the near-universal expectation is that it will hold the repo rate at 5.25 percent when it announces its decision on Friday. The question is not what the RBI will do this week. It is what it will tell the market about what comes next.

## The Case for Holding

A Mint poll of 10 economists found unanimous agreement: no change on June 5. The last rate cut was a 25-basis-point reduction in December 2025, back when inflation was below 4 percent and the Iran war had not yet begun.

Since then, the calculus has shifted dramatically. India has raised fuel prices four times in the past month. Brent crude, which was around $70 per barrel in late February, traded above $95 on Monday after Iran threatened to expand its Hormuz blockade to the Bab El Mandeb strait. The rupee has weakened to around ₹95 per dollar, though it recovered from ₹96.96 touched on May 20.

Yet the consensus remains that a rate hike would do more harm than good right now. CareEdge Ratings called the inflation uptick a "supply shock, not demand-driven," arguing that monetary tightening cannot fix a war-driven oil price spike. Axis Bank's Tanay Dalal was more direct: "The blunt tool of a rate hike is not well-suited to managing the currency."

## The Real Fight: Inflation vs Growth

The numbers tell a complicated story. Consumer inflation is still technically below the RBI's 4 percent target. But wholesale price inflation has spiked, raising fears of a "second-round pass-through" to retail prices — the scenario where higher input costs eventually flow into the prices consumers pay.

CareEdge projected GDP growth at 6.7 percent for FY27, assuming oil averages $90 per barrel. A prolonged war pushing crude to $110 could drag growth closer to 6 percent. SBI Research pegged growth at 6.6 percent and warned that CPI inflation could exceed 5 percent for the next three quarters.

The weak monsoon forecast adds another layer of concern. The India Meteorological Department is projecting the driest season in 11 years under a strengthening El Nino, threatening agriculture and food prices.

## What the RBI Will Signal

Emkay Global struck a more optimistic note, pointing to a 22 percent correction in Brent crude last month on hopes of a US-Iran framework. If the Strait of Hormuz reopens, the firm expects oil to settle at $75-80, giving the RBI room to hold for several quarters. SBI Research urged the central bank to use "short-term rates and nudging" rather than headline rate changes.

Market watchers will parse Governor Sanjay Malhotra's commentary for any shift in tone. The RBI maintained a "neutral" stance at its last meeting, preserving flexibility to move in either direction. If it shifts to a hawkish tilt, bond and currency markets will react.

## The Diaspora Impact

For NRIs with home loans, fixed deposits, or remittance planning tied to the rupee, the decision matters directly. A hold means EMIs stay stable and deposit rates remain attractive at current levels. But the longer-term signal — whether the RBI sees rate hikes as likely by year-end — will shape financial planning for the rest of 2026.

The 10-year bond yield ended last week at 7.00 percent after shedding 6 basis points, its biggest weekly decline since early April. Traders expect it to trade between 6.94 and 7.06 percent this week. The real volatility will come on Friday.

*Sources: Mint, IANS, CareEdge Ratings, Emkay Global, SBI Research, Outlook Money, Reuters*
author: Diaspora Desk
